clinical: Zone 3 is hit first
Oxygen falls from zone 1 to zone 3, so zone 3 is the first to be damaged when blood supply to the lobule falls, as in shock or heart failure.
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune disease that destroys the small bile ductules of the portal tracts. The result is cholestasis and, over time, scarring of the portal tracts.
Portal hypertension
Scarring that blocks blood flow through the liver, as in cirrhosis, raises pressure in the portal venous system. This is portal hypertension, which causes oesophageal varices and ascites.

Sinusoids.description: Sinusoids are the thin-walled, leaky blood channels between the hepatocyte plates, carrying mixed portal and arterial blood from the portal tract to the central vein. Their lining is made of flat, discontinuous endothelial cells with no basement membrane. Kupffer cells, the liver's macrophages, sit on the lumen side to clear bacteria and debris, while stellate (Ito) cells lie in the space of Disse, storing vitamin A and making extracellular matrix.
clinical: Liver scarring
When the liver is injured, stellate (Ito) cells are activated and lay down collagen, which is the main source of scarring in fibrosis and cirrhosis.
Capillarised sinusoids
In chronic liver disease the sinusoidal lining becomes capillarised, losing its fenestrae and gaining a basement membrane. This impairs exchange between the blood and the hepatocytes.
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Budd-Chiari syndrome is blockage of the hepatic veins, usually by thrombosis, so blood backs up into the central veins. It causes abdominal pain, an enlarged liver and ascites.
Right heart failure congestion
Raised pressure in the right heart is passed back through the hepatic veins to the central veins. Long-standing congestion gives the 'nutmeg' liver, with dark centrilobular congestion and necrosis.
Zone 3 injury

Centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis is the classic pattern of ischaemia and of congestive 'nutmeg' liver from right heart failure. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose also injures zone 3, because enzymes such as CYP2E1 there convert the drug into a toxic metabolite.
Zone 1 and zone 2 injury
Chronic viral hepatitis classically damages periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes, with interface (piecemeal) necrosis at the limiting plate. Yellow fever instead causes midzonal (zone 2) necrosis.
Jaundice and itching
If bile cannot drain, it regurgitates into the blood and causes jaundice and itching. A gallstone blocking the bile duct, or certain drugs, can cause this cholestasis.
Ductular reaction
After severe or repeated liver injury, progenitor cells in the canals of Hering proliferate, forming a ductular reaction that is seen on biopsy in chronic liver disease.

parts.description: Zone 2 (midzonal) hepatocytes are the liver cells in the broad middle band of each liver acinus (the functional unit of the liver), between the periportal zone 1 and the pericentral zone 3. Their oxygen supply and metabolism are intermediate between the two outer zones, and they are the cells damaged in midzonal necrosis, the characteristic liver lesion of yellow fever. In a section there is no sharp boundary, so this zone is recognised by its position midway between the portal tracts and the central veins.

Zone 1 (periportal) hepatocytes are the liver cells nearest the portal tracts, so they receive blood from the portal venule and hepatic arteriole first and are richest in oxygen and nutrients. They carry out gluconeogenesis (making glucose from non-carbohydrate sources), β-oxidation (breaking down fatty acids) and the urea cycle, and they are where viral hepatitis damage typically begins. In a section, they form the rim of cells lying beside each portal tract.

Hepatocyte nuclei are the large, round nuclei usually found near the centre of each liver cell, with finely dispersed chromatin and one or more visible nucleoli. Many hepatocytes are binucleate or polyploid, so a cell may contain two nuclei or one unusually large nucleus. In a section they appear as pale, round nuclei inside polygonal cells, which distinguishes them from the small, dark, flattened nuclei of the sinusoidal lining.

Inlet venules are small branches of the portal venule that run along the periphery of the lobule and pierce the limiting plate to empty into the sinusoids. They distribute portal blood directly into the liver plates, and they form the axis of the liver acinus, the line running between two portal tracts. In a section they look like small, thin-walled vessels at the edge of the lobule, where a portal tract meets the liver plates.

The central vein (terminal hepatic venule) lies at the centre of each lobule, with the sinusoids opening straight into its thin wall of endothelium, collagen and a few scattered smooth muscle cells. Blood from the central veins drains into the sublobular veins and then the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava. In a section it is recognised as a vessel with no portal tract beside it, surrounded by pericentral (zone 3) hepatocytes, and it can be blocked in veno-occlusive disease.

Sinusoidal endothelial cells are the flat, thin cells lining the sinusoids, perforated by small pores (fenestrae) that let plasma and small particles reach the hepatocytes. They have no basement membrane, so the space of Disse lies directly between them and the hepatocytes, and they take up and break down macromolecules by endocytosis. In a section they are seen as a thin lining of the sinusoid, and their flattened nuclei are usually the only part that stands out clearly.

Sinusoidal endothelial nuclei are the small, flat, dark-staining nuclei of the endothelial cells lining the sinusoids. They sit in the sinusoidal wall between neighbouring hepatocyte plates, so they appear as a row of thin, elongated nuclei along the edges of the sinusoids. Their dense chromatin and flattened shape contrast with the large, round, pale nuclei of hepatocytes, which helps you tell the two apart in a section.

Kupffer cells are the fixed macrophages of the liver, sitting inside the lumen of the sinusoids and attached to the endothelial lining. They belong to the mononuclear phagocyte system and engulf bacteria, bacterial toxins (endotoxin) and cell debris carried in the portal blood. In a section, look for irregular, star-shaped cells with an indented nucleus projecting into the blood channel, which may contain dark particles of ingested material.

Stellate (Ito) cells are the vitamin A-storing cells of the liver, lying in the space of Disse between the sinusoidal endothelium and the hepatocytes. Their cytoplasm holds lipid droplets rich in vitamin A, and they make collagen and other extracellular matrix, so when activated they become a key contributor to the scar tissue of fibrosis. In a section they are hard to pick out, but look for a cell with long processes running along the sinusoid wall.

The canalicular–Hering junction is the point at the limiting plate where a bile canaliculus joins the first segment of a canal of Hering. Here the lining changes from hepatocytes to cuboidal cholangiocytes (bile duct cells), and tight junctions seal the connection so that bile does not leak into the surrounding tissue. In a section, look for a tiny bile channel running from the edge of the lobule into a duct-like segment at the portal tract margin.

Bile ductules (also called interlobular bile ducts) are small bile ducts lying in the portal tracts beside the portal venules and hepatic arterioles, each lined by cuboidal cholangiocytes (bile duct cells) on a basement membrane. They carry bile from the canals of Hering towards the hilum, and in a section they look like small round profiles with a lumen and a thin ring of cuboidal cells. Their cells are destroyed in primary biliary cholangitis, and the ductules proliferate in large-duct obstruction.

Portal tract (portal canal) connective tissue: collagen of Glisson capsule that sheathes the portal venule, hepatic arteriole, bile ductule (the 'triad'), lymphatics and nerves at the corners of the lobule. Fibrous septa bridging portal tracts mark advanced fibrosis and are a key step towards cirrhosis.

Portal venules are the largest, thinnest-walled vessels of the portal tract, branches of the portal vein that carry blood from the gut and spleen into the liver. This blood is rich in nutrients but low in oxygen, and it makes up roughly three-quarters of the liver's blood flow. In a section, look for a large, thin-walled, often collapsed lumen beside the smaller, thick-walled hepatic arteriole.

Liver acinus zone 1 is the periportal part of the liver acinus, the diamond-shaped functional unit set between two portal tracts. Its hepatocytes lie nearest the inlet vessels, so they receive the best-oxygenated blood first and carry out gluconeogenesis and β-oxidation (fatty acid breakdown). In a section, zone 1 is the band of hepatocytes beside a portal tract, while zone 3 lies around the central veins.

Endothelial nuclear bulges are the thickened regions of the sinusoidal endothelial cells where the nucleus sits, and they push out into the sinusoid lumen. Elsewhere the endothelial cytoplasm is extremely thin, so the lining is mostly a flat sheet with these raised bulges standing out from it. In a section, they look like small nuclear-shaped bumps on the sinusoid wall that project into the blood channel.

Hepatocytes are the main functional cells of the liver, making up most of its cell mass, and they are polygonal with several flat faces. They are arranged in plates one or two cells thick, with a bile canalicular membrane on one side and a sinusoidal membrane on the other. In a section, look for polygonal cells with granular, pink cytoplasm and a round central nucleus, which distinguish them from the flattened cells of the sinusoidal lining.
